question: Why do you want to study Media and Communications?
lookingFor: A motivation grounded in specific experience with media rather than a vague love of 'talking to people' or 'being on camera'.

bullets: Point to a concrete experience that pulled you toward media, not a vague fondness for it
Show you understand the field covers more than presenting or social posting
Connect the interest to what you want to learn, not just what you enjoy consuming
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I got hooked running my school's Instagram account, where I had to figure out how to make a genuinely dull open-day announcement into something people actually stopped to read. That small problem, how you shape a message so it lands, turned into a bigger interest in how news outlets and brands do the same thing at scale, sometimes responsibly and sometimes not. I want to study the field properly because I've only been doing it by instinct, and I want the theory behind why some messages work and others fail.

commonMistakes: Saying 'I love social media' with nothing more specific
Framing it purely as wanting to be famous or on screen
Treating the degree as just journalism when it's broader
followUps: What part of media specifically, production, journalism, strategy, interests you most?

question: Why do you want to study Media and Communications here specifically, rather than at another university?
lookingFor: Evidence of real research into the specific course, its modules or facilities, not generic praise.

bullets: Name a specific module, studio facility, placement scheme, or faculty research area
Connect it to something concrete you've already done or want to do
Avoid language that could apply to any media course anywhere
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Your course has a dedicated module on media ethics and regulation in the second year, which most programs I looked at fold into one general lecture, and that's exactly the gap in my own thinking I want to fill. I also noticed the student-run radio station is fully integrated into the course rather than being an extracurricular add-on, and after two years producing a podcast at school I want that kind of consistent practical output alongside the theory. It felt like the course that takes production as seriously as it takes the critical side.

commonMistakes: Citing university ranking or reputation as the main reason
Describing features generic to most media courses
Being unable to name anything specific when pressed
followUps: What would you want to get involved with in your first term?

subtopic: The moment that sparked the interest
question: Was there a specific moment or experience that first got you interested in media and communications?
lookingFor: A genuine, specific anecdote that reveals real curiosity rather than a rehearsed origin story.

bullets: Describe one concrete moment rather than a general lifelong interest
Explain what specifically it made you notice or question
Show how it led to further action, not just a passing thought
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I remember watching two news channels cover the same protest completely differently, one calling it a riot and the other calling it a demonstration, and being genuinely unsettled that the same footage could be framed so differently. I started actively comparing how different outlets covered the same story, which is a habit I still have. That one afternoon is really what turned media from something I passively consumed into something I wanted to study properly.

commonMistakes: Claiming an interest 'since I was little' with no actual memory attached
Describing a moment that doesn't obviously connect to media
Stopping at the moment without showing what it led to
followUps: Have you kept up that habit of comparing coverage? What have you noticed recently?

question: What hands-on media experience have you had, whether that's a school paper, a podcast, video editing, or something else?
lookingFor: Real, specific experience with evidence of what you actually did and learned, not just a title held.

bullets: Name the specific role and what you actually produced
Give one concrete detail that shows real involvement, not a passive credit
Reflect on a skill or lesson it taught you
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I've edited for my sixth form's newspaper for two years, and last term I pitched and wrote a piece on our school's exam stress that ended up getting picked up by the local paper. Doing the interviews taught me how differently people speak when a recorder is out versus when you're just chatting, and I had to learn to build enough trust that they'd say something honest either way. It's the closest I've come to understanding what reporting actually feels like day to day, not just the finished article.

commonMistakes: Naming a club or role with no description of actual work done
Overstating a minor contribution as if it were a solo project
No reflection on what was learned from it
followUps: What would you do differently if you did that piece again?

subtopic: Wider reading and following the field
question: What have you read or listened to recently about the media industry, and what did you take from it?
lookingFor: Genuine, current engagement with the field beyond the school syllabus, with real reflection.

bullets: Name something specific and recent, not a vague 'I read the news'
Summarise the actual argument or finding, showing you understood it
Say what you personally took from it or where you disagreed
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I've been reading Nick Davies's 'Flat Earth News', about how commercial pressure on newsrooms leads to churnalism, reprinting press releases with barely any independent checking. What struck me was how much of it comes down to time and money rather than bad intentions, journalists aren't lazy, they're understaffed. It made me think differently about criticising outlets for shallow coverage, because the structural pressure behind it matters as much as the individual choices.

commonMistakes: Naming a source with no detail on its actual content or argument
Picking something clearly chosen only to sound impressive
Giving a summary with no personal reaction or opinion
followUps: Did you find yourself disagreeing with any part of it?

subtopic: A media figure or outlet they admire
question: Is there a journalist, presenter, or media outlet whose work you particularly admire? Why?
lookingFor: A specific, considered choice with reasons that go beyond popularity or charisma.

bullets: Name a specific person or outlet, not a vague category
Explain a specific quality of their work, not just that you like them
Show some awareness of their limitations too, if relevant
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I really admire the long-form investigative work Reuters does, particularly a piece they ran tracing a supply chain back through several countries with documents and interviews at every step. What I respect is the patience, that kind of story takes months and can't be rushed for a news cycle. I'm aware their access and resources put them in a different league to most outlets, but it's the standard I'd want to work toward.

commonMistakes: Naming someone famous with no specific reason attached
Praising style or personality alone with no substance
Being unable to name a single actual piece of their work
followUps: Is there anything about their approach you'd criticise?

subtopic: A story that stayed with them
question: Tell us about a piece of media coverage, a news story, documentary, or campaign, that has stuck with you. Why?
lookingFor: Specific, thoughtful engagement with a real piece of coverage, including some critical distance from it.

bullets: Name the specific piece and briefly what it covered
Explain what about the coverage itself, not just the topic, stayed with you
Bring some critical perspective, not pure praise
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A documentary on the collapse of a regional newspaper chain stuck with me, because it wasn't really about the news, it was about what a town loses when nobody's covering the school board meetings or the local court anymore. The bit that got me was a resident saying she found out about a factory closure from a neighbour, days after it happened, because there was no one left to report it. It reframed local journalism for me, from something I'd taken for granted to something closer to infrastructure.

commonMistakes: Discussing the topic itself rather than the coverage of it
Choosing something you can't actually describe in detail
Offering no personal reflection, just a summary
followUps: Do you think there's a solution to the local news problem you described?

question: What do you see as the key difference between journalism and public relations?
lookingFor: A clear grasp of the different goals and obligations of each, with awareness the line can blur.

bullets: State the core distinction: journalism serves the public's need to know, PR serves an organisation's interests
Note the difference in obligation, independence and verification versus advocacy
Acknowledge the blurred line, sponsored content, native advertising, PR-driven news
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Journalism is meant to serve the public by finding out and verifying what's true, even when that's uncomfortable for the people involved, while PR exists to represent an organisation's interests and present it in the best possible light. Neither is dishonest by definition, but their obligations point in different directions, a journalist's loyalty is to the audience, a PR professional's is to their client. What makes it complicated is how much journalism now relies on press releases and how much PR work mimics the tone of independent reporting, so the line isn't always obvious to a reader.

commonMistakes: Treating PR as simply 'lying' and journalism as simply 'truth'
Being unable to explain why the distinction matters practically
Ignoring how the two overlap in practice
followUps: Can you give an example of where that line gets blurred?

question: In your own words, what does 'media literacy' mean?
lookingFor: A clear, own-words definition with a practical example, not a textbook recitation.

bullets: Define it as the ability to access, analyse, and evaluate media critically, not just consume it
Mention questioning the source, purpose, and framing of a message
Give a concrete example of applying it
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: To me media literacy is the habit of asking who made this, why, and what they left out, rather than just absorbing a headline at face value. It's not about being cynical toward everything, it's about knowing the difference between a claim and evidence for it. I try to practice it by checking who funds a site before I trust a statistic it quotes, which has changed my mind about a few things I'd have otherwise just accepted.

commonMistakes: Defining it only as 'spotting fake news' and nothing broader
Giving a dictionary-style definition with no personal application
Confusing it with digital literacy or IT skills
followUps: How would you teach media literacy to someone younger than you?

question: Why do you think misinformation spreads so easily online, and what, if anything, can be done about it?
lookingFor: A reasoned view that touches on incentives, not just individual gullibility, plus realistic solutions.

bullets: Identify at least one structural driver, algorithms, emotional content, speed over verification
Avoid blaming users alone; show awareness of platform and business incentives
Offer a realistic, not utopian, idea for mitigation
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A lot of it comes down to what gets rewarded, content that provokes a strong emotional reaction spreads faster than a careful, hedged explanation, and platforms are built to maximise exactly that kind of engagement. It's not just that people are gullible, it's that the fastest, most shareable version of a story usually isn't the most accurate one. I don't think there's a single fix, but slowing sharing down, prompts that ask you to read before you share, for instance, has shown some real if modest effect, and I think media literacy education matters more long term than any platform tweak.

commonMistakes: Blaming only 'stupid people' with no structural analysis
Proposing censorship as a simple fix with no downsides considered
Vague hand-waving with no specific mechanism named
followUps: Should platforms be legally responsible for misinformation they host?

subtopic: Social media's effect on traditional media
question: How has social media changed the way traditional news organisations operate?
lookingFor: Awareness of concrete industry shifts, not just 'everything is faster now'.

bullets: Name a specific change, breaking-news speed, reliance on platform traffic, reporters as personal brands
Mention a real tension it creates for newsrooms
Show balanced awareness of both benefits and costs
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Newsrooms now compete with anyone holding a phone at the scene of a story, so speed has become a much bigger part of the job, sometimes at the expense of verification. It's also changed how outlets make money, a lot of traffic depends on platform algorithms they don't control, which is part of why several outlets have been badly hurt by a single Facebook algorithm change. On the positive side it's opened up direct access to sources and audiences that used to require expensive infrastructure, so it's not purely a loss, it's a real trade-off.

commonMistakes: Only naming speed without any deeper structural point
Treating the change as purely negative or purely positive
No concrete example to back the claim
followUps: Do you think that trade-off has been good or bad for journalism overall?

question: A source gives you damaging information about a public figure but only on condition of anonymity, and you can't independently verify it in time for publication. What do you do?
lookingFor: Structured ethical reasoning that weighs public interest, verification standards, and harm, not a snap decision.

bullets: Recognise the tension between a good story and unverified claims
Prioritise verification and corroboration over speed
Reason through the consequences of publishing wrongly versus holding the story
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: My instinct would be that a single anonymous source, however credible they sound, isn't enough on its own for something this damaging, because the cost of getting it wrong for the person involved is huge and hard to undo. I'd try to find at least one independent way to corroborate part of the claim, documents, a second source, anything, before running with it, even if that means missing being first. If I genuinely couldn't verify it in time, I'd hold the story rather than publish, because being right matters more than being fast, and I'd rather lose a scoop than get a real person's life wrong.

commonMistakes: Publishing immediately because the story is compelling
Refusing to ever use anonymous sources at all, which is unrealistic
Not considering the harm of publishing something false
followUps: Would your answer change if a rival outlet was about to publish it first?

question: Where do you think the line should be drawn between a public figure's right to privacy and the public's right to know?
lookingFor: Nuanced reasoning that distinguishes genuine public interest from mere public curiosity.

bullets: Draw a distinction between 'interesting to the public' and 'in the public interest'
Give a test or principle, relevance to the person's public role or duties
Acknowledge genuinely hard edge cases rather than pretending the line is always clear
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think the useful question isn't whether the public is curious, it's whether the information bears on something the person's public role gives them power over, a politician's undeclared financial interests are fair game because they affect how they vote, but their child's private medical history generally isn't. That said, I know it's genuinely messy in practice, a politician's personal conduct can sometimes reveal something real about their judgement or hypocrisy, so I don't think there's a clean formula, more a habit of asking what the story actually reveals about their public duties before running it.

commonMistakes: Claiming public figures simply forfeit all privacy
Refusing to engage with any hard cases
No workable principle offered, just vague discomfort
followUps: Does a public figure's family, who didn't choose public life, deserve more protection?

question: What do you understand by the term 'gatekeeping' in media studies?
lookingFor: A working understanding of the concept and how it's changed with digital platforms.

bullets: Define gatekeeping as the process by which editors decide what news gets published and how
Note it shapes public awareness by what's included and excluded, not just what's said
Reference how social platforms and algorithms have added new, less visible gatekeepers
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Gatekeeping is the idea that editors and producers act as filters, deciding which stories reach an audience and which don't, which quietly shapes public understanding just as much as how a story is written. What I find interesting is how that role hasn't disappeared with the internet, it's just shifted, an algorithm deciding what appears in a feed is doing a version of the same job, except with far less transparency about how the decision is made. So the gate still exists, it's just moved somewhere less visible.

commonMistakes: Defining it only as literal censorship
Failing to connect it to algorithmic curation today
No example given to ground the definition
followUps: Do you think algorithmic gatekeeping is more or less accountable than editorial gatekeeping?

question: Do you think true objectivity in journalism is actually possible?
lookingFor: A thoughtful, non-cynical view that recognises the limits of objectivity without dismissing journalistic standards altogether.

bullets: Acknowledge that pure neutrality is hard given every choice, what to cover, which words, is a decision
Distinguish objectivity as a practical discipline (fairness, verification) from an unreachable ideal
Avoid the trap of concluding that bias makes all reporting equally untrustworthy
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I don't think perfect objectivity is really achievable, because even choosing what counts as a story worth covering is already a judgement call, and word choice can lean a piece one way without anyone lying. But I don't think that makes objectivity a useless standard, it's more like a discipline, checking facts, representing the strongest version of opposing views, being transparent about sourcing, that keeps reporting honest even if it can't be perfectly neutral. Treating all coverage as equally biased because none of it is perfectly objective feels like it throws out something genuinely valuable.

commonMistakes: Claiming journalism is either perfectly neutral or entirely useless, no middle ground
Confusing objectivity with simply presenting 'both sides' regardless of evidence
Giving a purely cynical answer with no defence of journalistic standards
followUps: Is 'both-sidesism' always the same thing as objectivity?

question: What role do you think the media should play in a functioning democracy?
lookingFor: A clear articulation of at least one function beyond 'informing people', with awareness of tension with commercial pressures.

bullets: Name a specific function, holding power to account, informing decisions, providing a shared public forum
Acknowledge the tension between that role and commercial or political pressures
Avoid an idealised view detached from how the industry actually operates
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think its core job is holding power accountable, making it harder for institutions to act badly in the dark, alongside just informing people so they can actually make decisions as voters and citizens. What's tricky is that this role depends on outlets having the resources and independence to do difficult investigative work, and commercial pressure often pushes in the opposite direction, toward whatever is cheap and gets clicks. So I think the ideal and the reality are often in tension, and that tension is part of what makes the industry interesting to study rather than something already solved.

commonMistakes: A purely idealised answer with no acknowledgment of commercial reality
Reducing the media's role to entertainment alone
No specific function named, just vague talk of 'informing the public'
followUps: Can a fully commercial media system still perform that role well?

question: What do you understand by 'media convergence', and can you give an example?
lookingFor: A correct grasp of convergence as the merging of previously distinct media forms and platforms, backed by a real example.

bullets: Define convergence as the blending of previously separate media technologies, industries, and content types
Give a real, specific example rather than a vague one
Note an effect it has, on audiences, on how outlets produce content, or on business models
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Media convergence is the way different forms of media, text, video, audio, that used to live on separate platforms with separate business models have merged into the same spaces. A newspaper's website now runs video explainers and podcasts alongside written articles, all produced by what's increasingly one integrated newsroom rather than separate departments. It means journalists today are often expected to be multi-skilled across formats, which is a real shift from how the industry used to be organised.

commonMistakes: Confusing convergence with simply 'the internet exists'
Giving no concrete example
Missing the industry or audience-side effect of the concept
followUps: Do you think convergence has made journalism better or has spread it too thin?

question: What's a current trend in media or communications that you find interesting, and why?
lookingFor: Genuine, up-to-date engagement with the industry, with a specific reason it matters, not just naming a buzzword.

bullets: Name a specific, current trend rather than something already old news
Explain what's actually changing and why it matters
Give a personal reaction or opinion on it, not just description
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I've been following how much news consumption is shifting toward short vertical video on platforms like TikTok, and how outlets that used to see that as beneath them are now building whole teams around it. What interests me is the format itself forces a completely different kind of storytelling, you have maybe three seconds to earn attention, which changes what stories even get told that way. I'm honestly a bit torn on it, it's clearly reaching audiences traditional formats were losing, but I worry about what gets left out when everything has to fit fifteen seconds.

commonMistakes: Naming a trend that's actually years old and treating it as new
Describing the trend with no personal opinion attached
Being unable to explain why it's actually significant
followUps: Do you think that trend is good or bad for the quality of journalism overall?

question: Why does understanding your target audience matter when creating media content or a communications campaign?
lookingFor: Practical understanding that message effectiveness depends on the audience's needs, not just the creator's intent.

bullets: Explain that the same message can succeed or fail depending on who receives it and how
Mention a factor that shapes audience needs, platform habits, values, prior knowledge
Ideally back it with a real or hypothetical example
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The same information can land completely differently depending on who's receiving it, a public health message written for doctors would confuse and probably alienate a general audience even if every fact in it is correct. When I ran our school's Instagram account I learned this the hard way, a long, formal caption I was proud of got almost no engagement, while a short, casual one about the same event did far better, because I'd finally matched the tone to how people actually scroll. It taught me that a message isn't really finished until you've thought about who's on the other end of it.

commonMistakes: Treating audience as an afterthought rather than central to the message
Giving a purely abstract answer with no concrete example
Assuming one message works equally well for everyone
followUps: How would you research an audience you didn't know well before creating content for them?

question: How would you go about identifying bias in a news article, beyond just checking which outlet published it?
lookingFor: A concrete, transferable method for critical reading, not just 'know which outlets are biased'.

bullets: Name specific textual signals: word choice, which voices are quoted, what's placed first versus buried
Mention checking what's omitted, not only what's included
Show this is a habit applied to any source, including ones you agree with
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd look at word choice first, whether the language is loaded or neutral, and then at whose voices actually get quoted directly versus paraphrased or left out entirely, because that shapes sympathy even when the facts are accurate. I'd also check what's placed high up versus buried near the end, since burying an inconvenient detail is a subtler kind of bias than leaving it out completely. The habit I try hardest to keep is applying that same scrutiny to sources I already agree with, because that's exactly where I'm least likely to notice it on my own.

commonMistakes: Reducing bias-detection to simply checking the outlet's known political lean
Naming only one signal instead of a real method
Implying they only apply scrutiny to outlets they already distrust
followUps: Can a piece be factually accurate and still be biased? How?

question: Should there ever be limits on press freedom, or should the press be free to report anything it wants?
lookingFor: A balanced position that recognises legitimate limits, national security, defamation, without endorsing broad censorship.

bullets: Reject both absolutist extremes, unlimited freedom and broad state control
Name a legitimate, narrow category of limit, e.g. defamation, incitement to imminent violence, and explain why
Show awareness that 'limits' are easily abused to silence legitimate reporting
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I don't think press freedom should be unlimited, publishing something knowingly false that destroys someone's reputation, or details that would directly get a source killed, has real victims and I think narrow limits like defamation law exist for good reason. But I'm genuinely wary of broader limits, because 'national security' or 'public order' get used constantly by governments to bury stories that are simply embarrassing rather than actually dangerous. So my honest answer is some limits are legitimate, but they need to be narrow, clearly defined, and not something the government itself gets to decide case by case.

commonMistakes: An absolutist answer either way, with no engagement with the hard middle ground
Failing to notice how easily 'security' justifications get abused
No specific example or category of limit named
followUps: Can you think of a real case where you think a government used security as a pretext for censorship?

question: Can you briefly explain a basic model of communication, sender, message, receiver, and where it can break down?
lookingFor: A correct, simply explained basic model with a real understanding of where noise or misinterpretation enters.

bullets: Describe the basic chain: a sender encodes a message, it travels through a channel, a receiver decodes it
Name 'noise' or context as the thing that can distort meaning along the way
Give a concrete everyday example of the breakdown
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The simplest version is a sender encodes an idea into a message, sends it through some channel, and a receiver decodes it, but that decoding depends on the receiver's own context, so meaning can shift along the way. What we usually call 'noise' isn't just literal noise, it can be cultural assumptions or prior beliefs that change how a message lands. A sarcastic tweet is a good example, the sender's intended tone can get completely lost once it's stripped of vocal inflection and read by someone with a different context.

commonMistakes: Describing only the sender and receiver with no mention of distortion or noise
Confusing this basic model with something more advanced without grounding it first
No real example to illustrate where meaning can break down
followUps: How does that model change once you add something like social media into the channel?

subtopic: AI and the future of media
question: How do you think artificial intelligence is changing, or will change, journalism and the wider media industry?
lookingFor: A balanced, specific view of both opportunities and risks, not an overly simple 'AI will replace journalists' or 'AI is just a tool' answer.

bullets: Name a specific current use, automated financial reporting, transcription, personalised recommendation
Identify a real risk, synthetic media, deskilling, job displacement in specific roles, not journalism broadly
Land on a considered, not alarmist or dismissive, overall view
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: It's already doing real work in places like automated earnings reports and transcription, which frees up time for the harder investigative work that actually needs a person. What worries me more is synthetic media, video and audio convincing enough that verification becomes much harder, right when trust in media is already fragile. I don't think it replaces the core of journalism, judgement, relationships with sources, deciding what matters, but I do think it's going to reshape which entry-level jobs exist, and that's worth taking seriously rather than dismissing.

commonMistakes: A purely alarmist 'AI will replace all journalists' answer with no nuance
A dismissive 'it's just a tool, nothing changes' answer with no specifics
No concrete current example given
followUps: How would you personally verify whether a piece of video or audio evidence is genuine?

question: Tell us about a time someone gave you tough feedback on something you'd written or produced. How did you respond?
lookingFor: Genuine openness to criticism and evidence of actually improving the work, not defensiveness dressed up as growth.

bullets: Describe specific, real feedback, not a softened or invented version
Show the initial reaction honestly, including any defensiveness, before the shift
Explain the concrete change made and what resulted
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: My editor on the school paper once told me a piece I'd worked on for weeks buried the actual point in paragraph six, and my first reaction was defensive, I thought the buildup was necessary. But when I reread it with her note in mind I could see she was right, I'd been more attached to my own structure than to whether a reader would actually get to the point. I rewrote the opening to lead with the finding and moved the context after, and it read a hundred times better, which taught me to separate how attached I am to a draft from whether it actually works.

commonMistakes: Describing feedback that was actually praise in disguise
Staying defensive throughout with no real acknowledgment of the critique
No specific detail on what was actually changed
followUps: How do you now try to get feedback earlier, before a piece is finished?

subtopic: Goals and how the course connects
question: What kind of role in media or communications do you see yourself working toward, and how does this course get you there?
lookingFor: A grounded direction, not necessarily one fixed job title, with a clear, specific line to what the course offers.

bullets: Give a direction or area of interest rather than an over-precise single job title
Name specific skills or knowledge from the course that build toward it
Show flexibility, awareness that the exact path may shift
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'm drawn to investigative or long-form reporting, the kind of work that takes months rather than hours, though I know the industry is narrow and I might end up somewhere adjacent like a research or fact-checking role first. This course's mix of practical production modules and a strong grounding in media law and ethics feels like exactly the foundation that kind of work needs, since getting it wrong legally or ethically can end a story, or a career, fast. I'm open to the exact path shifting, but the combination of rigorous training and real production experience is what I think gets me closest to it.

commonMistakes: An overly rigid, unrealistically specific career plan
A goal with no clear link back to what the course actually teaches
Sounding uncertain about wanting to work in the field at all
followUps: What's the first step you'd want to take toward that goal after graduating?
